spark.summary: Low-Level Design (LLD) translates high-level requirements into clean class hierarchies, explicit state machines, concurrency-safe interfaces, and extensible design patterns inside a single service or library.
spark.keyTakeaway: Great LLD isolates volatile business rules behind narrow interfaces and explicit state transitions so adding a new rule never requires rewriting core orchestration.

concept.whyItMatters: While High-Level Design (HLD) decides how services communicate over networks, Low-Level Design determines whether a codebase stays maintainable at 100k+ lines and thread-safe under 10,000 concurrent requests. Poor LLD produces god classes, race conditions on shared state, and brittle `if/else` chains that break on every new feature.
whenToUse: Designing core domain engines inside a service (e.g., rate limiters, order matching engines, parking-lot/elevator schedulers, notification dispatchers).
Building shared SDKs, plugin architectures, or payment/pricing pipelines where new strategies must be added without modifying callers (Open/Closed Principle).
Modeling workflows with strict lifecycle invariants (e.g., `CREATED → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → REFUNDED`) that must resist concurrent duplicate requests.
whenNotToUse: Writing one-off migration scripts or 100-line glue utilities where heavy abstractions add indirection without reuse.
Prematurely introducing 6 layers of AbstractFactory/Bridge patterns before a second concrete implementation or variation point actually exists.
Trying to solve cross-service distributed consensus or network partitioning problems purely through in-memory OOP patterns.
keyPoints: Separate entities (identity + lifecycle), value objects (immutable, equality by value), and stateless domain services.
Model lifecycles as explicit Finite State Machines (FSMs) with validated transition tables rather than scattered boolean flags (`isPaid`, `isCancelled`, `isRefunded`).
Use Strategy, State, Observer, and Command patterns to invert dependencies so core orchestration depends on interfaces/Protocols, never concrete vendors.
Design concurrency boundaries explicitly: define which objects are immutable, which use fine-grained locks (`ReentrantLock` per entity ID), and which use atomic compare-and-set.
Keep public APIs narrow and idempotent, enforcing invariants in constructors/factories so invalid domain states cannot be instantiated.

examples.title: Multi-Tier Rate Limiter Engine
examples.scenario: An API gateway must support Token Bucket for bursty clients, Sliding Window Log for strict billing endpoints, and per-tenant hot-swapping.
examples.outcome: Defining a `RateLimiter` interface with `allow(key, tokens)` and injecting `Clock` + `BucketStore` enabled unit-testing time deterministically in < 1 ms and adding Leaky Bucket with zero changes to middleware.

examples.title: Thread-Safe Parking Lot & Spot Allocator
examples.scenario: Multiple entry gates concurrently assign compact, EV, and large spots while exit gates free spots and compute tiered fees.
examples.outcome: Partitioning locks per floor (`ReentrantLock`), separating `SpotAllocationStrategy` (Nearest-to-Gate vs. Load-Balanced) from `PricingStrategy`, and using immutable `Ticket` value objects eliminated double-allocation races.

tradeOffs.pro: Strategy and Dependency Injection make swapping algorithms, mocking clocks/stores, and adding variants trivial.
tradeOffs.con: Over-abstracting stable code scatters simple logic across dozens of tiny files and slows onboarding.

tradeOffs.pro: Locking per entity/shard (e.g., striped `ReentrantLock` by `accountId`) preserves high multi-core throughput.
tradeOffs.con: Multi-entity operations (transfers) risk deadlocks unless a strict global lock-acquisition order is enforced.

tradeOffs.factor: Rich Domain Objects vs. Anemic Data Models
tradeOffs.pro: Encapsulating invariants inside domain methods prevents callers from mutating objects into illegal states.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit DTO/entity mapping at persistence and serialization boundaries.

failureModes.name: Boolean Flag Explosion & Illegal States
failureModes.description: Tracking `isActive`, `isPaused`, and `isDeleted` as independent booleans allows impossible combinations like `isActive=true && isDeleted=true`.
failureModes.mitigation: Replace flags with a single enum-backed State Machine and an explicit `(currentState, event) → nextState` transition map.

failureModes.name: Check-Then-Act Race Condition
failureModes.description: Two threads check `spot.isFree()` simultaneously, both see `true`, and both issue tickets for the same resource.
failureModes.mitigation: Make check-and-reserve atomic inside a per-entity lock, optimistic version check, or CAS transition.

failureModes.name: Deadlock on Multi-Resource Acquisition
failureModes.description: Thread A locks Account 1 then Account 2 while Thread B locks Account 2 then Account 1.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce deterministic lock ordering (e.g., always lock `min(id1, id2)` before `max(id1, id2)`) or use `tryLock` with timeout.

failureModes.name: God Class Orchestrator
failureModes.description: A single 2,000-line `OrderManager` owns validation, pricing, inventory, notifications, and persistence, breaking on every edit.
failureModes.mitigation: Split along Single Responsibility boundaries into cohesive domain services, strategies, and repository ports.

commonMistakes: Hardcoding `System.currentTimeMillis()` or `time.time()` inside core logic instead of injecting a `Clock` interface for deterministic tests.
Exposing mutable internal collections (`getItems()`) that let callers bypass domain validation.
Using inheritance (`Car extends Vehicle`, `ElectricCar extends Car`) where composition (`Vehicle` + `Powertrain` + `SizingSpec`) avoids diamond hierarchies.
Ignoring thread safety on shared caches, registries, or singleton pools.
Designing around database tables first instead of modeling behaviors, invariants, and state transitions.

sections.content:
## The idea

Low-Level Design (LLD) is the discipline of structuring in-process modules, classes, interfaces, and concurrency primitives so a system is **correct under concurrency**, **easy to test deterministically**, and **open to extension without rewriting core flows**.

Instead of treating code as CRUD wrappers around database rows, strong LLD models:
- **Boundaries**: Narrow interfaces (ports) separating domain logic from clocks, storage, and external SDKs.
- **Invariants**: State machines and immutable value objects that make illegal states unrepresentable.
- **Variation Points**: Composition-based patterns (Strategy, State, Command, Observer) isolating the parts of the domain most likely to change.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through designing an extensible **Order & Payment Processor** in Java/Python:

1. **Value Objects & FSM**: Define `Money(amountMinorUnits, currency)` as an immutable value object (never `float` for currency) and `OrderStatus` as a strict FSM (`PENDING → RESERVED → PAID → SHIPPED`, or `→ CANCELLED`).
2. **Dependency Inversion**: `OrderService` accepts `InventoryPort`, `PaymentStrategy` (Card, UPI, Wallet), and `DomainEventBus` via constructor injection.
3. **Concurrency Guard**: Acquire a striped lock keyed by `orderId` (or optimistic `version` CAS) before transitioning `PENDING → RESERVED` so duplicate webhook/retry calls cannot double-charge.
4. **Event Emission**: On successful `PAID` transition, publish `OrderPaidEvent` to `DomainEventBus` so `EmailNotifier` and `AnalyticsTracker` react asynchronously without polluting `OrderService`.

sections.content:
## Core principles & pattern selection

Choose patterns to eliminate specific structural pain rather than to check a textbook box:

- **Composition over Inheritance**: Favor small capability interfaces (`Flyable`, `Chargeable`) or strategy objects over deep class trees that break when a hybrid type appears.
- **Explicit Time & Randomness**: Inject `Clock` and `IdGenerator` everywhere so rate limiters, TTL caches, and schedulers run deterministically in unit tests without `Thread.sleep()`.
- **Immutability by Default**: Make DTOs, events, and value objects (`Money`, `TimeRange`, `Coordinate`) immutable so they can be shared across threads with zero defensive copying.

## LLD pattern selection matrix

| Pattern | Problem Solved | Concrete Example | When to Avoid |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategy** | Swapping algorithms at runtime without `if/else` | Surge pricing, eviction policy (LRU/LFU), payment rails | Only 1 static algorithm exists |
| **State (FSM)** | Eliminating illegal transitions across booleans | Order lifecycle, elevator states, circuit breaker (`OPEN/HALF_OPEN/CLOSED`) | Simple 2-state active/inactive toggle |
| **Observer / EventBus** | Decoupling side effects from core mutations | Triggering SMS, audit log, and loyalty points on checkout | Strictly ordered transactional steps |
| **Command** | Encapsulating actions for undo, queuing, or audit | Text editor undo stack, delayed job scheduler | Direct synchronous method calls |
| **Factory / Builder** | Enforcing invariants on complex multi-field creation | Constructing validated HTTP requests or SQL query specs | Simple 2-field structs |

## Failure modes

1. **Circular Package Dependencies**: `orders` imports `payments` and `payments` imports `orders`, preventing independent compilation or testing. *Mitigation*: Extract shared interfaces/events into a lower-level `contracts` or domain kernel module.
2. **Leaky Abstractions**: A `StoragePort` interface exposes `ResultSet` or Redis-specific `ZRANGE` errors, forcing callers to change when migrating backends. *Mitigation*: Map vendor exceptions into domain-level errors at the adapter boundary.
3. **Unbounded In-Memory State**: Caching every session or rate-limit key in a plain `HashMap` without eviction leaks memory until OOM. *Mitigation*: Bound maps with LRU/TTL eviction or background sweeping.
4. **Non-Idempotent Side Effects Under Retry**: Sending an email or charging a card inside a lock that times out and retries causes duplicate actions. *Mitigation*: Attach idempotency keys to commands and separate state commit from outbox/event dispatch.

## Testing & concurrency verification

Good LLD makes testing effortless:

- **Unit Tests (< 5 ms)**: Test state transitions, edge cases, and pricing math in-memory with fake repositories and a controllable `ManualClock`.
- **Concurrency Stress Tests**: Spawn 16–32 threads hammering shared allocators or rate limiters with a `CountDownLatch`/`CyclicBarrier` to catch race conditions and deadlocks.
- **Contract Tests**: Run the exact same test suite against both in-memory test doubles and real SQL/Redis adapters to guarantee behavioral parity.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Identify core entities, immutable value objects, and explicit state-machine transitions.
- [ ] Isolate volatile rules (pricing, routing, eviction) behind narrow Strategy/Port interfaces.
- [ ] Inject `Clock`, `Random`, and `IdGenerator` instead of calling static globals.
- [ ] Define locking granularity (per-entity striped locks or CAS) and enforce deterministic lock ordering for multi-entity ops.
- [ ] Verify zero illegal states can be constructed and test concurrent paths with multi-threaded barrier tests.

steps.explanation: Low-Level Design (LLD) translates high-level requirements into clean class hierarchies, explicit state machines, concurrency-safe interfaces, and extensible design patterns inside a single service or library.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: PaymentStrategy Port applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Repo & EventBus.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Repo & EventBus experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Replace flags with a single enum-backed State Machine and an explicit `(currentState, event) → nextState` transition map.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Great LLD isolates volatile business rules behind narrow interfaces and explicit state transitions so adding a new rule never requires rewriting core orchestration.
Avoid trap: Hardcoding `System.currentTimeMillis()` or `time.time()` inside core logic instead of injecting a `Clock` interface for deterministic tests.
Avoid trap: Exposing mutable internal collections (`getItems()`) that let callers bypass domain validation.
When to reach for it: Designing core domain engines inside a service (e.g., rate limiters, order matching engines, parking-lot/elevator schedulers, notification dispatchers).
When to reach for it: Building shared SDKs, plugin architectures, or payment/pricing pipelines where new strategies must be added without modifying callers (Open/Closed Principle).

putItTogether.title: Putting Low Level Design Systems Together
putItTogether.summary: Great LLD isolates volatile business rules behind narrow interfaces and explicit state transitions so adding a new rule never requires rewriting core orchestration.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Low Level Design Systems before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Defining a `RateLimiter` interface with `allow(key, tokens)` and injecting `Clock` + `BucketStore` enabled unit-testing time deterministically in < 1 ms and adding Leaky Bucket with zero changes to middleware.
